blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html:
Reliability is the degree to which an instrument gives consistent, reproducible results: across occasions, across items meant to measure the same thing, or across raters. It says nothing about whether the instrument measures the right thing.

In classical test theory each observed score X is a true score T plus a random error E, uncorrelated with T:

X = T + E, so σ²_X = σ²_T + σ²_E

The reliability coefficient is the share of observed-score variance that is true-score variance:

r_xx = σ²_T ÷ σ²_X = σ²_T ÷ (σ²_T + σ²_E)

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: The miscalibrated scale of §16.2 reads 2 kg too high every time. That consistency is reliability. Reliability of 0.80 means that 80% of the spread in observed scores reflects real differences between people and 20% reflects noise. It runs from 0 (all noise) to 1 (no noise).

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html: A questionnaire given twice, a week apart, to the same stable patient should give nearly the same score both times if it is reliable, whether or not that score reflects the intended construct.

points.html: Reliability is consistency, not correctness. §16.4 shows that it caps validity.

Four types follow, each asking “consistent across what?”: items within one administration (internal consistency, §16.3.1); the same instrument on two occasions (test-retest, §16.3.2); different raters (inter-rater, §16.3.3); two equivalent versions (parallel forms, §16.3.4). §16.3.5 then asks a related question: do two measurement methods agree?
Reliability is a property of scores in a particular population, not of the instrument alone. The same instrument is less reliable in a population where true scores vary less, because σ²_T is smaller.

blocks.html: Internal Consistency Reliability

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: Internal consistency reliability is the degree to which the items of one scale, all meant to measure the same construct, correlate with each other in a single administration.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: If a 10-item satisfaction scale measures one construct, someone who agrees that “staff were respectful” should tend to agree that “I would recommend this facility”. Internal consistency checks whether the items hang together as they should.

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html: If half the items of a satisfaction scale correlate strongly with each other but poorly with the other half, either the scale measures two constructs (a dimensionality problem that principal component analysis, §16.5, can show) or some items are badly worded.

points.html: It needs only one administration. Test-retest needs two.

The item-total correlation is the correlation between one item and the total score. The corrected item-total correlation (SPSS “corrected item-total correlation”, R r.drop) correlates the item with the total of the other items, so the item does not correlate with itself. A value near zero or negative marks an item that does not belong or was not reverse-coded. Tavakol & Dennick (2011) advise that items whose correlation with the total is low, “approaching zero”, are deleted.
Low internal consistency can mean the scale is not unidimensional, items are poorly worded, or there are too few items. Each needs a different fix.

blocks.html: Cronbach’s Alpha

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html:
Cronbach’s alpha estimates internal consistency reliability from the item variances and the variance of the total score. For a scale of k items, with item variances sᵢ² and total-score variance s_T²:

α = [k ÷ (k − 1)] × (1 − Σsᵢ² ÷ s_T²)

(Bland & Altman, 1997). Standardised alpha uses the mean inter-item correlation r̄ instead:

α_std = k r̄ ÷ [1 + (k − 1) r̄]

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: The total score’s variance is the sum of the item variances plus twice every covariance between items. If the items measure one construct, they covary positively, the covariances make up a large share of the total variance, and Σsᵢ² ÷ s_T² is small, so α is high. If the items are unrelated, the covariances are near zero, s_T² ≈ Σsᵢ², and α is near 0. If the items covary negatively, s_T² is smaller than Σsᵢ², the bracket goes negative, and so does α.

blocks.label: Derivation
blocks.html:
1. T = X₁ + X₂ + … + X_k. Expanding Var(T) = E[(T − E[T])²] gives the variance of a sum: Var(T) = ΣVar(Xᵢ) + 2 Σ₍ᵢ<ⱼ₎ Cov(Xᵢ, Xⱼ) (covariance recalled from §11.2).
  2. So 1 − Σsᵢ² ÷ s_T² = (2 Σ covariances) ÷ s_T², the share of total variance that comes from items moving together.
  3. There are k(k − 1)/2 covariances but k variances. The factor k/(k − 1) rescales so that α = 1 when all items are perfectly correlated with equal variances.
  4. With standardised items (each variance 1, each covariance r̄): s_T² = k + k(k − 1) r̄. Substituting gives α_std = k r̄ ÷ [1 + (k − 1) r̄]. This is the Spearman–Brown formula, the reliability of a total of k parallel items each correlating r̄.

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html:
Five patients answer three satisfaction items on a 1–5 scale:

Patient Item 1 Item 2 Item 3 Total
1 4 5 4 13
2 5 4 5 14
3 3 4 2 9
4 2 2 3 7
5 1 2 1 4

blocks.label: Worked Calculation
blocks.html:
1. Item means 3.0, 3.4, 3.0. Sums of squared deviations 10.0, 7.2, 10.0, so the variances (÷ 4) are s₁² = 2.5, s₂² = 1.8, s₃² = 2.5. Σsᵢ² = 6.8.
  2. Totals 13, 14, 9, 7, 4: mean 9.4, sum of squared deviations 69.2, s_T² = 69.2 ÷ 4 = 17.3.
  3. Check: covariances 1.75, 2.25 and 1.25, and 6.8 + 2 × (1.75 + 2.25 + 1.25) = 6.8 + 10.5 = 17.3.
  4. α = (3 ÷ 2) × (1 − 6.8 ÷ 17.3) = 1.5 × (1 − 0.393) = 1.5 × 0.607 = 0.91.
  5. Inter-item correlations are 0.825, 0.900 and 0.589, so r̄ = 0.771. α_std = 3 × 0.771 ÷ (1 + 2 × 0.771) = 2.314 ÷ 2.543 = 0.91. It matches raw α here because the item variances are similar.
  6. Negative alpha. Suppose item 3 were a reverse-worded item (“I felt ignored”) entered without recoding, so each score is 6 minus the value shown. Its variance stays 2.5, but its covariances with items 1 and 2 become −2.25 and −1.25. Then s_T² = 6.8 + 2 × (1.75 − 2.25 − 1.25) = 3.3, smaller than Σsᵢ², and α = 1.5 × (1 − 6.8 ÷ 3.3) = 1.5 × (−1.061) = −1.59. A negative α is a red flag, usually for an item that was not reverse-coded.

Alpha and scale length. Hold r̄ at 0.3. Spearman–Brown gives α_std = 0.56 for 3 items, 0.81 for 10 and 0.90 for 20. Alpha rises with k only while r̄ is held. Add five items that correlate only 0.05 with the rest to a 10-item scale (r̄ = 0.3). The mean inter-item correlation of the 15 items falls to (45 × 0.3 + 60 × 0.05) ÷ 105 = 0.157, and α_std falls from 0.81 to 0.74.

...

item2      0.95      0.95    0.90      0.90 18.0    0.047    NA  0.90

raw_alpha 0.91 is step 4 and std.alpha 0.91 is step 5, with average_r 0.77 as r̄. The alpha-if-item-deleted column recomputes α with each item left out. Dropping item 2 would raise α to 0.95, and item 2 has the lowest corrected item-total correlation (r.drop 0.73). That makes it the first candidate for review, though with 5 respondents this is only a teaching example.

points.html: Alpha usually lies between 0 and 1, but it has no lower bound. Streiner (2003) lists “restricted to the range of 0 to 1” among four myths about alpha. A negative value means the items covary negatively on average: check reverse-coding first.

Conventional thresholds (conventions, not laws): α of 0.7 to 0.8 is “satisfactory” for comparing groups, and at least 0.90 is wanted for decisions about individual patients (Bland & Altman, 1997). Terwee et al. (2007) rate internal consistency positively when α lies between 0.70 and 0.95. A very high α (above about 0.90 to 0.95) may mean redundant items that ask the same question in different words (Tavakol & Dennick, 2011).
Holding the mean inter-item correlation constant, α rises with the number of items (Spearman–Brown). A long scale can reach a high α with weak items. Adding poorly correlated items can lower α.
Alpha assumes one dimension. A scale made of two unrelated sub-scales can still show a respectable α (Tavakol & Dennick, 2011). Check dimensionality first (§16.5) and report α for each sub-scale.
Alpha belongs to the scores in one sample, not to the instrument. Compute it again in each new study population.

blocks.html: Test-Retest Reliability

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: Test-retest reliability is the degree to which the same instrument, given to the same unchanged respondents on two occasions, gives consistent scores. For continuous scores it is quantified by an intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC). For categorical scores it is quantified by kappa (agreement corrected for chance, §16.3.3.1).

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html:
Internal consistency looks for agreement within one administration, across items. Test-retest looks for agreement across time with the same instrument, assuming nothing real has changed. The ICC (recall §15.2.1, where it measured clustering) is the share of total variance due to real differences between subjects:

ICC = σ²_subjects ÷ (σ²_subjects + σ²_other)

The forms differ in what counts as “other” (Shrout & Fleiss, 1979; the documentation of R’s psych package maps them to SPSS labels):

Form Design What counts as error SPSS label
ICC(1) One-way: each subject measured by different, random occasions or raters All within-subject variation, including any systematic shift One-way random, absolute agreement
ICC(2,1) Two-way random: occasions or raters are a sample from a wider set Random error plus systematic shift between occasions Two-way random, absolute agreement
ICC(3,1) Two-way mixed: these particular occasions or raters are fixed Random error only; a constant shift is ignored Two-way mixed, consistency

“k” versions (ICC(1,k), ICC(2,k), ICC(3,k)) give the reliability of the average of k measurements.

blocks.label: Derivation
blocks.html:
Lay out n subjects × k occasions and partition the sums of squares as in two-way ANOVA (recall §9.5.1 for mean squares and §9.5.4 for the two-way layout). MS_S is the between-subjects mean square, MS_O the between-occasions mean square, MS_E the residual, and MS_W the pooled within-subject mean square (occasion plus residual):

ICC(1) = (MS_S − MS_W) ÷ [MS_S + (k − 1) MS_W]

ICC(2,1) = (MS_S − MS_E) ÷ [MS_S + (k − 1) MS_E + k (MS_O − MS_E) ÷ n]

ICC(3,1) = (MS_S − MS_E) ÷ [MS_S + (k − 1) MS_E]

Only ICC(2,1) and ICC(1) carry the occasion effect in the denominator. A systematic shift between occasions lowers them. It leaves ICC(3,1) untouched.

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html:
A knowledge questionnaire is given to 5 ASHA workers twice, a week apart. Between the two sessions, their supervisor unexpectedly discussed the topic with them.

Worker Week 1 Week 2 Difference
1 10 14 4
2 14 19 5
3 18 22 4
4 22 27 5
5 26 30 4

blocks.label: Worked Calculation
blocks.html:
1. Grand mean 20.2. Subject means 12, 16.5, 20, 24.5, 28. Occasion means 18.0 and 22.4.
  2. SS_S = 2 × Σ(subject mean − 20.2)² = 2 × 160.3 = 320.6, df 4, so MS_S = 80.15.
  3. SS_O = 5 × [(18.0 − 20.2)² + (22.4 − 20.2)²] = 5 × 9.68 = 48.4, df 1, so MS_O = 48.4.
  4. SS_total = 369.6, so SS_E = 369.6 − 320.6 − 48.4 = 0.6, df 4, and MS_E = 0.15. MS_W = (48.4 + 0.6) ÷ 5 = 9.8.
  5. ICC(3,1) = (80.15 − 0.15) ÷ (80.15 + 0.15) = 80.0 ÷ 80.3 = 0.996.
  6. ICC(2,1) = 80.0 ÷ [80.3 + 2 × (48.4 − 0.15) ÷ 5] = 80.0 ÷ (80.3 + 19.3) = 80.0 ÷ 99.6 = 0.80.
  7. ICC(1) = (80.15 − 9.8) ÷ (80.15 + 9.8) = 70.35 ÷ 89.95 = 0.78.
  8. Pearson’s r between the weeks is 0.996.

Every worker scored 4 or 5 points higher in week 2. The ranking was preserved, so r and the consistency ICC(3,1) are almost 1. The absolute-agreement ICC(2,1) drops to 0.80 because a respondent’s week-1 score does not reproduce their week-2 score. For test-retest reliability, where a score should repeat, absolute agreement is the relevant question.

blocks.label: In R (optional)
blocks.html:
library(psych)
retest <- data.frame(week1 = c(10, 14, 18, 22, 26),
                     week2 = c(14, 19, 22, 27, 30))
cor(retest$week1, retest$week2)
ICC(retest)
[1] 0.996271
...
                         type  ICC     F df1 df2     p lower bound upper bound
Single_raters_absolute   ICC1 0.78   8.2   4   5 2e-02      0.0508        0.97
Single_random_raters     ICC2 0.80 534.3   4   4 1e-05     -0.0022        0.98
Single_fixed_raters      ICC3 1.00 534.3   4   4 1e-05      0.9647        1.00
...

The three single-measure rows reproduce steps 5–7 (ICC3 prints as 1.00 after rounding 0.996). The confidence interval for ICC2 runs from about 0 to 0.98: with 5 subjects almost nothing is pinned down.

points.html: Choose the interval with care. Too short, and respondents remember and repeat their answers, which inflates the estimate. Too long, and real change in the construct (or, as here, an intervening event) deflates it.
Use only for constructs expected to stay stable over the interval. Retesting momentary mood measures real change, not unreliability.

Always name the ICC form (model, type, single or average). Koo & Li (2016) note that there are 10 forms of ICC and ask authors to report “model”, “type” and “definition”. They also propose bands based on the 95% CI: below 0.5 poor, 0.5–0.75 moderate, 0.75–0.9 good, above 0.9 excellent (a convention). Terwee et al. (2007) rate reliability positively when the ICC or weighted kappa (kappa with partial credit for near misses, §16.3.3.1) is at least 0.70 in at least 50 patients.

Within-subject SD and repeatability. When there is no systematic shift, the within-subject SD is s_w = √MS_E. The difference between two measurements of one person has SD √2 × s_w. So 95% of repeat differences fall within 1.96 × √2 × s_w = 2.77 s_w, the repeatability coefficient.

blocks.html: Inter-Rater Reliability

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: Inter-rater reliability is the degree to which two or more independent raters, assessing the same subjects with the same instrument, agree.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: The attention moves from the instrument to the people using it. A well-designed instrument can still give inconsistent results if one nurse grades a wound “mild” and another grades the same wound “moderate”.

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html: Two community health workers independently classify the nutritional status of the same 50 children with the same criteria. How often, and how closely, do they agree?

points.html: Test-retest compares the same instrument on two occasions. Inter-rater compares different raters on the same subjects at one time.
Categorical ratings: Cohen’s kappa (§16.3.3.1). Continuous ratings: the ICC, in the forms of §16.3.2, with raters in place of occasions.
Poor agreement usually points to training, instructions or unclear scoring criteria.

blocks.html: Cohen’s Kappa

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html:
Cohen’s kappa measures agreement between two raters on categorical ratings, corrected for the agreement expected by chance:

κ = (pₒ − pₑ) ÷ (1 − pₑ)

where pₒ is the observed proportion of agreement and pₑ is the proportion expected if the two raters rated independently at their own observed rates.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: Two raters agree some of the time by chance alone, especially with few categories. Kappa removes that part. The numerator is agreement beyond chance. The denominator is the most agreement beyond chance that was possible.

blocks.label: Derivation
blocks.html:
If the raters rate independently, the probability that both say “anaemic” is (A’s proportion anaemic) × (B’s proportion anaemic), by the multiplication rule for independent events (recall §5.2.2). The same holds for “not anaemic”. Adding over categories:

pₑ = Σ (row proportion × column proportion)

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html:
Two medical officers independently classify 100 women attending an antenatal clinic as anaemic or not anaemic, by clinical pallor alone.

B: anaemic B: not anaemic Row total
A: anaemic 11 10 21
A: not anaemic 5 74 79
Column total 16 84 100

blocks.label: Worked Calculation
blocks.html:
1. pₒ = (11 + 74) ÷ 100 = 0.85.
  2. A calls 21% anaemic and B calls 16%. Chance agreement on “anaemic” = 0.21 × 0.16 = 0.0336. On “not anaemic” = 0.79 × 0.84 = 0.6636.
  3. pₑ = 0.0336 + 0.6636 = 0.697 (about 0.70).
  4. κ = (0.85 − 0.697) ÷ (1 − 0.697) = 0.153 ÷ 0.303 = 0.50 (0.505 to 3 dp).

An 85% raw agreement shrinks to κ = 0.50. Most of the agreement is on “not anaemic”, which both raters say most of the time, so chance alone would produce much of it.

Interpreting kappa. Landis & Koch (1977, p. 165) proposed these labels, reproduced in the Stata manual:

κ Strength of agreement
below 0.00 Poor
0.00–0.20 Slight
0.21–0.40 Fair
0.41–0.60 Moderate
0.61–0.80 Substantial
0.81–1.00 Almost perfect

On this scale κ = 0.50 is “moderate”. The bands are a convention. The 95% CI, 0.29 to 0.72, comes from a large-sample SE of κ that is usually left to software; the rough hand version, SE ≈ √[pₒ(1 − pₒ)/n] ÷ (1 − pₑ) = 0.118, gives 0.27 to 0.74. The interval runs from “fair” to “substantial”, so the label is uncertain.

The prevalence paradox. Keep pₒ = 0.85 and change only how common the condition is:

Table (a / b / c / d) A “yes” B “yes” pₑ κ
45 / 10 / 5 / 40 (balanced) 0.55 0.50 0.50 0.70
11 / 10 / 5 / 74 (this clinic) 0.21 0.16 0.697 0.50
80 / 10 / 5 / 5 (very common) 0.90 0.85 0.78 0.32

The same 85% agreement gives κ from 0.70 to 0.32. When one category dominates, pₑ is high and kappa is low: “a high value of p₀ can be drastically lowered by a substantial imbalance in the table’s marginal totals” (Feinstein & Cicchetti, 1990).

The bias paradox. Keep pₒ = 0.85 and the clinic’s 11 and 74 agreements, but move all 15 disagreements to one side (A says anaemic, B not: 11 / 15 / 0 / 74). A now calls 26% anaemic and B 11%. pₑ = 0.26 × 0.11 + 0.74 × 0.89 = 0.687, and κ = (0.85 − 0.687) ÷ 0.313 = 0.52. Kappa rises even though the raters now disagree systematically. Byrt, Bishop & Carlin (1993) recommend reporting “quantitative indicators of bias and prevalence” alongside kappa, such as the two raters’ marginal proportions. A related index, the prevalence-adjusted bias-adjusted kappa (PABAK), recomputes kappa as if pₑ were 0.5 (balanced categories, no bias): PABAK = (pₒ − 0.5) ÷ 0.5 = 2pₒ − 1, here 2 × 0.85 − 1 = 0.70.

Weighted kappa for ordered categories. Plain kappa treats “normal vs severe” as no worse than “normal vs moderate”. Weighted kappa (Cohen, 1968) gives partial credit to near misses. Two anganwadi supervisors grade 60 children as normal, moderate acute malnutrition (MAM) or severe acute malnutrition (SAM):

B: normal B: MAM B: SAM Total
A: normal 30 4 0 34
A: MAM 3 12 2 17
A: SAM 1 2 6 9
Total 34 18 8 60
  1. Unweighted: pₒ = 48 ÷ 60 = 0.80. Expected diagonal counts (row × column ÷ 60) are 19.27, 5.10 and 1.20, so pₑ = 25.57 ÷ 60 = 0.426, and κ = (0.80 − 0.426) ÷ 0.574 = 0.65.
  2. Linear agreement weights: 1 on the diagonal, 0.5 one category apart, 0 two apart. Observed weighted agreement = (48 + 0.5 × 11 + 0 × 1) ÷ 60 = 53.5 ÷ 60 = 0.892.
  3. Expected: the one-apart cells have expected counts 10.2, 9.63, 2.27 and 2.70 (total 24.8). pₑ(w) = (25.57 + 0.5 × 24.8) ÷ 60 = 37.97 ÷ 60 = 0.633.
  4. κ_w = (0.892 − 0.633) ÷ (1 − 0.633) = 0.70.

Eleven of the twelve disagreements are only one grade apart, so the weighted kappa is higher. With quadratic weights (the default in R’s psych package) κ_w is 0.76. State which weights you used.

k <- read.csv("data/kappa_anaemia.csv")
tab <- table(rater_A = k$rater_A, rater_B = k$rater_B)
tab

                 3, 12, 2,

cohen.kappa(whz, w = abs(outer(1:3, 1:3, "-")) / 2)   # linear weights

rater_A       anaemic not anaemic
  anaemic          11          10
  not anaemic       5          74
...
                 lower estimate upper
unweighted kappa  0.29      0.5  0.72
...
                 lower estimate upper
unweighted kappa  0.48     0.65  0.82
weighted kappa    0.54     0.70  0.87

The first table is the 2×2 above, and the kappa estimate 0.5 (95% CI 0.29 to 0.72) is step 4. For the malnutrition grades, the unweighted 0.65 and linearly weighted 0.70 match steps 1–4. The w argument holds disagreement weights (0 on the diagonal, 0.5 and 1 off it), the complement of the agreement weights used by hand.

points.html: κ = 1 is perfect agreement, 0 is chance-level agreement, and negative values mean agreement worse than chance. The lower limit depends on the marginals and is not always −1.
Report pₒ, both raters’ marginal proportions and κ with its CI, not κ alone (Byrt et al., 1993).
More than two raters: Fleiss’ kappa extends the chance correction to more than two raters. The raters need not be the same people for every subject (Stata kappa manual).

Kappa and McNemar’s test (recall §10.8) answer different questions about the same 2×2 table. McNemar asks whether one rater says “yes” more often than the other (bias, using only the discordant cells b and c). Kappa asks how well they agree beyond chance.

blocks.html: Parallel-Forms Reliability

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: Parallel-forms reliability is the correlation between scores on two different but equivalent versions of an instrument given to the same respondents.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: Retesting with the same items lets respondents remember answers and practise, which inflates test-retest reliability. Two forms with different but equivalent items remove memory and practice effects. They also expose error from item sampling: how much a score depends on which particular items were chosen.

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html: Two equivalent 20-item knowledge tests (Form A and Form B) are given to the same medical students. A high correlation supports parallel-forms reliability. The two forms can then be used for pre- and post-training tests without students simply recalling Form A.

points.html: Building two equivalent forms is a heavy development burden, which limits the use of this design.

questions.prompt: A researcher gives the same questionnaire to the same patients twice, two weeks apart, and finds a high correlation. Which type of reliability is this? Name one threat that would inflate the estimate and one that would deflate it, even for a well-designed instrument.
questions.answer: Test-retest reliability. Inflating: respondents remember and repeat their first answers (memory or practice effects), especially with a short interval. Deflating: real change in the construct between occasions (for example, a patient’s anxiety actually improving), or an intervening event such as health education. A low value does not by itself show the instrument is unreliable. Note also that a correlation ignores a systematic shift between occasions, so ICC(2,1) is preferred (§16.3.2).

questions.prompt: A four-item scale has item variances 1.2, 1.0, 1.5 and 1.3 and total-score variance 12.0. Compute Cronbach’s alpha. A ten-item scale has α = 0.97. What might this very high value signal?
questions.answer:
1. Σsᵢ² = 1.2 + 1.0 + 1.5 + 1.3 = 5.0.
  2. α = [4 ÷ 3] × (1 − 5.0 ÷ 12.0) = 1.333 × 0.583 = 0.78, satisfactory for group comparisons by the Bland & Altman (1997) convention.

α = 0.97 on ten items may mean redundancy: several items ask the same question in different words, adding length without new information. Terwee et al. (2007) rate α positively only up to 0.95. Also, α rises with the number of items (Spearman–Brown), so a high value partly reflects length. It does not show that the scale is unidimensional or valid.

questions.prompt: Two nurses classify 200 children as “fever” or “no fever” by touch. Both say fever for 30, neither for 140, nurse A only for 20, nurse B only for 10. Compute pₒ, pₑ and κ, and give the Landis & Koch label.
questions.answer:
1. pₒ = (30 + 140) ÷ 200 = 0.85.
  2. Nurse A says fever for (30 + 20) ÷ 200 = 0.25; nurse B for (30 + 10) ÷ 200 = 0.20.
  3. pₑ = 0.25 × 0.20 + 0.75 × 0.80 = 0.05 + 0.60 = 0.65.
  4. κ = (0.85 − 0.65) ÷ (1 − 0.65) = 0.20 ÷ 0.35 = 0.57: “moderate” (0.41–0.60) on the Landis & Koch (1977) scale, a convention. Report the two marginal proportions too: nurse A calls fever more often (bias), and fever is the minority category (prevalence), both of which affect κ.

blocks.html: Agreement Between Two Methods – Bland–Altman

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html:
A Bland–Altman analysis asks whether two methods of measuring the same continuous quantity agree well enough to be used interchangeably. For each subject, compute the difference d between the two methods. Report the bias (the mean difference, d̄) and the 95% limits of agreement:

d̄ ± 1.96 × s_d

where s_d is the SD of the differences (Bland & Altman, 1986). The limits give the range within which about 95% of differences between the two methods are expected to lie. The Bland–Altman plot graphs each difference against the mean of the two readings.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: A PHC wants to replace its mercury sphygmomanometer with a digital device. The question is not “are the readings related?” (they must be: both measure the same blood pressure). The question is “by how much can a digital reading differ from the mercury reading for the same person?” If that range is clinically unimportant, the methods can be swapped. That judgement is clinical, not statistical: you decide beforehand how large a difference would matter.

blocks.label: Derivation
blocks.html:
1. Let dᵢ = digital − mercury for subject i. If the differences are roughly Normal with mean μ_d and SD σ_d, then 95% of them lie within μ_d ± 1.96σ_d (recall the Normal distribution, §5.7.2.2).
  2. Estimate μ_d by d̄ and σ_d by s_d. This gives the limits d̄ ± 1.96 s_d.
  3. d̄ is a sample mean, so its SE is s_d ÷ √n and its 95% CI is d̄ ± t₀.₉₇₅,ₙ₋₁ × s_d ÷ √n (recall §7.2.1). If the CI excludes 0, the bias is systematic, which is the same as a paired t-test (recall §9.2.3).
  4. Why r is the wrong statistic (recall §11.2): r measures how closely points lie along any straight line. If the digital reading were always mercury + 10 mmHg, r would be 1 while every reading was 10 mmHg wrong. r also rises with the spread of the true values in the sample, which has nothing to do with agreement.

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html: Thirty adults at a PHC have systolic BP measured with both a mercury sphygmomanometer and a digital device (data/bp_methods.csv). Mean SBP is 129.0 mmHg by mercury and 133.5 mmHg by digital.

blocks.label: Worked Calculation
blocks.html:
1. Differences (digital − mercury): d̄ = +4.53 mmHg, s_d = 4.95 mmHg.
  2. Limits of agreement: 4.53 − 1.96 × 4.95 = −5.2 mmHg and 4.53 + 1.96 × 4.95 = 14.2 mmHg.
  3. SE(d̄) = 4.95 ÷ √30 = 0.903. With t₀.₉₇₅,₂₉ = 2.045, the 95% CI for the bias is 4.53 ± 2.045 × 0.903 = 2.69 to 6.38 mmHg. It excludes 0, so the digital device reads systematically higher.
  4. Pearson’s r between the methods is 0.95, although individual readings differ by up to 17 mmHg.
  5. Reading: for a given adult, the digital device may read from about 5 mmHg lower to 14 mmHg higher than mercury. A 14 mmHg over-reading can move a person across the systolic threshold of 140 mmHg at which WHO diagnoses hypertension (on two different days; WHO, 2025), so the two methods are not interchangeable for diagnosis without correction.

blocks.alt: Bland–Altman plot of digital minus mercury systolic BP
blocks.caption: Figure 16.1. Bland–Altman plot for 30 adults. Each point is one adult: the difference between the digital and mercury readings against their mean. The solid line is the bias (+4.53 mmHg), the dashed lines the 95% limits of agreement (−5.2 and 14.2 mmHg). Two of the 30 points lie outside the limits, about the 5% expected.

blocks.label: In R (optional)
blocks.html:
library(psych)
bp <- read.csv("data/bp_methods.csv")
d <- bp$sbp_digital - bp$sbp_mercury
m <- (bp$sbp_digital + bp$sbp_mercury) / 2
c(bias = mean(d), sd = sd(d))
mean(d) + c(-1.96, 1.96) * sd(d)
t.test(d)$conf.int
cor(bp$sbp_mercury, bp$sbp_digital)
cor(d, m)
ICC(bp[, c("sbp_mercury", "sbp_digital")])
plot(m, d)
abline(h = mean(d) + c(-1.96, 0, 1.96) * sd(d), lty = c(2, 1, 2))
    bias       sd 
4.533333 4.946147 
[1] -5.161114 14.227781
[1] 2.686412 6.380255
[1] 0.9530262
[1] 0.0519762
...
                         type  ICC  F df1 df2       p lower bound upper bound
Single_raters_absolute   ICC1 0.92 23  29  30 1.0e-13        0.83        0.96
Single_random_raters     ICC2 0.92 41  29  29 7.2e-17        0.58        0.97
Single_fixed_raters      ICC3 0.95 41  29  29 7.2e-17        0.90        0.98
...

The first four lines are steps 1–4. cor(d, m) = 0.05 shows that the differences do not grow with the level of BP, so a single pair of limits fits the whole range. (If they did grow, you would analyse log-transformed readings or ratios.) The ICCs repeat the lesson of §16.3.2: the consistency ICC(3,1), 0.95, ignores the 4.5 mmHg bias, while the absolute-agreement ICC(2,1), 0.92, is lower and has a much wider lower confidence bound (0.58). No ICC tells you, in mmHg, how far apart two readings can be. Only the limits of agreement do.

points.html: The limits of agreement are estimates too. Var(d̄) = s_d²/n, and the SD itself has sampling variance of about s_d²/2n (proof beyond this book), so each limit has SE ≈ √(s_d²/n + 1.96² × s_d²/2n) ≈ √(3s_d²/n). Here that is √(3 × 4.95² ÷ 30) = 1.56 mmHg: the upper limit’s 95% CI is about 14.2 ± 2.045 × 1.56, or 11.0 to 17.4 mmHg. Thirty subjects pin the limits down only roughly.
Always look at the plot. A funnel shape (differences widening with the mean) or a slope means one pair of limits misdescribes the agreement.
A regression of one method on the other and a paired t-test each answer only part of the question: the paired t-test detects bias but says nothing about the spread of individual differences.
A method can be compared with itself: two readings by the same method give the repeatability coefficient of §16.3.2.

questions.prompt: A new haemoglobinometer and the laboratory cyanmethaemoglobin method are compared in 40 pregnant women. Mean difference (new − lab) is −0.3 g/dL, SD of differences 0.6 g/dL. Compute the 95% limits of agreement. The study defines anaemia as Hb below 11 g/dL: interpret the limits for a woman whose laboratory value is 11.2 g/dL.
questions.answer:
1. Lower limit = −0.3 − 1.96 × 0.6 = −0.3 − 1.18 = −1.48 g/dL.
  2. Upper limit = −0.3 + 1.96 × 0.6 = −0.3 + 1.18 = 0.88 g/dL.

For about 95% of women, the new device reads between 1.48 g/dL below and 0.88 g/dL above the laboratory. For a woman whose laboratory value is 11.2 g/dL, the device could plausibly read anywhere from about 9.7 to 12.1 g/dL, so she could be labelled anaemic or not. The device under-reads on average (bias −0.3 g/dL) and is too imprecise to replace the laboratory for individual diagnosis near the cut-off, unless the investigators judged a difference of about 1.5 g/dL clinically acceptable beforehand.

questions.prompt: The same study reports r = 0.96 between the two methods and concludes “excellent agreement”. What is wrong with this conclusion?
questions.answer: r measures how closely the points lie along some straight line, not whether the readings are equal. It would be 1 even if the device always read exactly 1 g/dL low. It also rises when the women’s true haemoglobin values vary widely, which says nothing about agreement. Agreement is assessed by the bias and limits of agreement (Bland & Altman, 1986), as in question 1.
